questions.title: Tell me about yourself in a Node.js architect interview
questions.quick: I would give a ninety-second story in three beats. First, my background: many years in software engineering, growing from building backend services in Node.js, TypeScript and NestJS into designing APIs, microservices, event-driven flows and PostgreSQL data models. Second, the kind of systems I have worked on: enterprise and SaaS platforms with security, reliability and maintainability needs. Third, why this role fits: it combines backend architecture, cloud and distributed systems, and governance, which is where I want to apply my experience.
questions.revision: Three beats: background and stack, the kind of systems and outcomes, why this role. Keep it to about ninety seconds and end by linking your strengths to the role.
questions.detailed:
The opening question is not a request for a biography. It is a chance to frame the rest of the interview, so a good answer is short, structured and pointed at the role.

## A three-beat structure
1. **Who you are professionally.** Years of experience, the core stack (for example Node.js, TypeScript, NestJS, PostgreSQL) and how your responsibilities grew from building features to designing systems.
2. **What you have delivered.** The kind of systems (enterprise applications, SaaS, regulated domains), and the engineering concerns you care about: scalability, security, maintainability, release discipline. Use one concrete outcome rather than a list of technologies.
3. **Why this role.** Connect the job description (backend architecture, cloud, distributed systems, governance) to what you want to do next.

## What to include and what to leave out
| Include | Leave out |
|---|---|
| Scope of decisions you owned | Every project in chronological order |
| One measurable or observable outcome | Technology lists with no context |
| Interest in the role's specific themes | Personal details, complaints about past employers |
| A hook the interviewer can follow up on | Claims you cannot support in depth |

## Handling skills you are still building
If the role names a platform you have used less (a particular cloud, for example), say so plainly in the follow-up discussion rather than implying depth you do not have. Explain the transferable concepts you do know, such as networking, identity, managed databases and messaging, and say you would validate service-specific limits and costs against current documentation.

## Common mistakes
- Reciting a resume line by line for five minutes.
- Staying purely technical and never stating the business impact.
- Ending without saying why you want this particular role.
- Over-rehearsing so the answer sounds scripted; know the beats, not the sentences.

## Example (hypothetical skeleton)
"I am a software engineer and architect with many years in backend development, mostly Node.js and TypeScript with NestJS. I design APIs and microservices, use event-driven patterns where they help, and model data in PostgreSQL. I have worked on enterprise and SaaS platforms where security and reliability mattered, and I enjoy turning ambiguous requirements into clear service boundaries and delivery plans. This role interests me because it joins backend architecture, distributed systems and governance."
followUps: Which of those projects are you proudest of, and why?
What was the hardest architectural decision you made?
How has your role changed from developer to architect?

questions.title: Why should we hire you as a Node.js architect?
questions.quick: I would say an architect turns business requirements into architecture that meets both functional and non-functional needs, then stays involved until it runs reliably in production. I bring backend depth, design experience and technical leadership. I define service boundaries, API contracts, data strategy, security standards, pipeline controls and observability, and I justify decisions with trade-offs and measurable targets, not trends. Where a platform is newer to me, I apply the underlying concepts and validate service-specific behaviour, limits and cost before committing.
questions.revision: Connect business requirements, sound architecture, implementation quality and operational reliability. Back every claim with a trade-off or a measurable target.
questions.detailed:
"Why should we hire you" tests whether you understand what the role is for. Answer with the value an architect creates, then show evidence you can create it, instead of listing adjectives.

## What an architect is hired to do
- Translate business requirements into an architecture that satisfies functional needs and non-functional ones (latency, availability, security, recoverability, cost).
- Define service boundaries, API contracts, data ownership and integration patterns.
- Guide implementation so the design survives contact with the codebase.
- Keep the system reliable in production through observability, release controls and incident learning.

## A structure for the answer
| Part | What you say |
|---|---|
| Fit | Backend depth in the stack the team uses, plus design and leadership experience |
| Method | You decide with requirements and trade-offs, record decisions, and prefer the simplest design that meets measurable targets |
| Delivery | You stay close to code, reviews and production behaviour |
| Honesty | You name areas where you will ramp up and say how you will validate them |

## Pragmatism as a selling point
Many teams are hurt by complexity that no business need justified. Saying you choose boring, well-understood solutions until a requirement forces something heavier is a strength, provided you can describe when you would escalate (for example moving from a modular monolith to separate services).

## Being honest about gaps
If the role uses a cloud platform you know less well, do not claim fluency. Say that the core concepts (identity, networking, managed data stores, messaging, deployment) transfer, and that you would check service-specific behaviour, quotas and pricing against current documentation and a small proof of concept before relying on them.

## Common mistakes
- Listing technologies instead of outcomes.
- Presenting architecture as slideware with no link to code or operations.
- Overclaiming on tools you have not used in depth.
- Ignoring the team: architects succeed by raising other engineers' decisions, not by deciding everything.

## Example (hypothetical)
"For a platform like this, I would start by agreeing availability and data-sensitivity targets with the business, propose service boundaries and an API-first contract approach, and set standards for security, CI/CD checks and tracing. I would write short decision records for the choices we make, review the first implementations against them, and adjust as production data arrives."
followUps: What would you do in your first ninety days?
Tell me about a design decision you later regretted.
How do you handle a team that disagrees with your design?

questions.title: How do you approach architecture design end to end?
questions.quick: I start with the business goal and gather functional requirements, expected traffic, security constraints, availability targets, data sensitivity and budget. From those I define measurable non-functional requirements. Then I draw domain boundaries, data ownership and integration contracts, and decide what is synchronous and what is asynchronous. I compare a few options, record the choice in a decision record, and cover security, deployment, observability and disaster recovery. Finally I validate with prototypes, load tests, threat modelling and an operational-readiness review.
questions.revision: Requirements, constraints, options, documented trade-offs, validation, then governance. Measurable non-functional targets come before technology choices.
questions.detailed:
A strong answer shows a repeatable process, not a favourite technology. The sequence below works for most backend and platform designs.

{{diagram:flow}}

## 1. Understand the problem
Clarify business goals, users, functional scope, expected traffic and growth, regulatory and security constraints, data sensitivity, team skills and budget. Ask what happens if the system is down or wrong.

## 2. Turn constraints into measurable non-functional requirements
Examples: p95 latency target, availability target, recovery time and data-loss tolerance, throughput, consistency needs, audit requirements. Unmeasured words such as "fast" or "secure" cannot be designed against.

## 3. Shape the structure
Identify domain boundaries and data ownership, define API and event contracts, and decide where interaction is synchronous and where asynchronous messaging is safer.

## 4. Compare options
Evaluate two or three candidates (for example a modular monolith versus services) against the requirements. Capture the decision, alternatives and consequences in a short **architecture decision record**.

## 5. Cover cross-cutting concerns
Security (identity, authorisation, encryption, secrets), deployment and release strategy, observability, backup and disaster recovery, cost.

## 6. Validate before committing
| Technique | Risk it reduces |
|---|---|
| Prototype or spike | Unknown technical feasibility |
| Load test | Missed throughput or latency targets |
| Threat modelling | Security design gaps |
| Operational-readiness review | Surprises on the first incident |

## 7. Govern and evolve
Review implementations against the decisions, track technical debt, and revisit decisions when assumptions change.

## Common mistakes
- Choosing technology first and justifying it later.
- Designing for imagined scale and adding needless complexity.
- Leaving operations, security and recovery to "later".
- Producing a design nobody can trace to a requirement.

## Example (hypothetical)
For an internal document-approval service expecting a few hundred users, the targets might be 99.9% availability and one-hour recovery. That points to a modular monolith, a managed PostgreSQL instance with backups, asynchronous notifications through a queue, and a simple pipeline, with a record of why microservices were deferred.

diagrams.alt: A left to right sequence: requirements, non-functional targets, structure and boundaries, options and decision records, cross-cutting concerns, validation, then governance.

questions.title: What is the difference between a senior developer and an architect?
questions.quick: I would say a senior developer delivers reliable solutions within a defined scope, with strong code quality and mentoring. An architect owns system-level decisions and their consequences: dependencies between services, security, reliability, scalability, deployment, cost, team capability and long-term evolution. The roles overlap, and the best architects stay close to the code and to production behaviour, because a design that ignores how the system actually runs is just a diagram.
questions.revision: Senior developer: excellent delivery within a scope. Architect: owns cross-system decisions and their long-term consequences, while staying close to code and production.
questions.detailed:
Both roles are technical and both lead. The difference is the **scope of the decisions** and the **time horizon of their consequences**.

## Comparison
| Aspect | Senior developer | Architect |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | A service, feature area or component | Several systems, shared platforms and boundaries between teams |
| Primary output | Working, well-tested code and sound local design | Decisions, contracts, standards and guardrails others build within |
| Time horizon | Current release and near-term maintainability | Years of evolution, migration and operating cost |
| Trade-offs | Code structure, performance, testability | Security, availability, cost, team skills, vendor and platform choices |
| Influence | Reviews, mentoring, example by code | Alignment across teams, decision records, technical strategy |
| Accountability | Quality of delivered work | Whether the overall system meets its non-functional goals |

## Where they overlap
Good architects keep reading code, reviewing pull requests and looking at production telemetry. Good senior developers make architectural decisions daily within their component. The title matters less than whether someone is accountable for cross-cutting outcomes.

## What architects do that is easy to miss
- Say "no" or "not yet" to unnecessary complexity.
- Make decisions reversible where possible and record the irreversible ones.
- Create alignment so teams do not each solve integration differently.
- Plan for operations: monitoring, failure modes, recovery, cost.

## Common mistakes
- The "ivory tower" architect who hands down designs without code contact.
- The architect who becomes a bottleneck by approving everything.
- Treating the move to architect as a promotion away from engineering rather than a change of focus.

## Example (hypothetical)
A senior developer designs how an orders service handles retries and validates input. An architect decides whether orders, payments and inventory should be separate services, which events they publish, what consistency they promise each other, and what the recovery target is for the whole flow. Each needs the other's insight.
followUps: How do you stay hands-on as an architect?
How do you influence teams that do not report to you?
When should a senior developer step into architecture work?
